title: Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia: Recognition and Emergency Surgical Pathway
specialty: Vascular Surgery / General Surgery / Emergency Medicine

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI) in the emergency department (ED), surgical ward or intensive care unit (ICU): recognition of the four types (arterial embolism, arterial thrombosis, non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia and mesenteric venous thrombosis), laboratory tests, computed tomography angiography (CTA), resuscitation, heparin, antibiotics and the surgical or endovascular pathway. Uses the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) 2022 guideline, the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) intra-abdominal infection protocol and US product labels. Operative technique is for the surgical team and is summarised only.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-21.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi acute mesenteric ischaemia guideline was found; WSES 2022 is used, with the Saudi MOH protocol for antibiotic choice.

WSES 2022 gives no heparin dose; the label full-dose regimen is shown. WSES gives a post-operative activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) range of 40 to 60 without stating units (seconds assumed).
WSES 2022 names no antibiotic; piperacillin–tazobactam is taken from the MOH protocol severe-infection column, which does not mention mesenteric ischaemia.
Typical adult normal ranges for lactate, white cell count, D-dimer, amylase and potassium are not from WSES; local laboratory ranges apply.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: AMI is a sudden loss of blood supply to the bowel that progresses to necrosis; mortality exceeds 50% if untreated (WSES 2022, Background). Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) embolism from the heart is the classic cause; thrombosis occurs on chronic atherosclerotic stenosis at the vessel origin (WSES 2022, Pathophysiology). Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI) is SMA vasoconstriction from low splanchnic flow in heart failure, sepsis, hypovolaemia or vasopressor use (WSES 2022, Pathophysiology). Mesenteric venous thrombosis (MVT) follows Virchow's triad, for example thrombophilia, pancreatitis or recent surgery (WSES 2022, Pathophysiology). Ischaemia starts in the mucosa and spreads to the serosa, so pain precedes abdominal signs; peritonitis means likely bowel necrosis (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).

symptoms: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).
Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; blood per rectum in about 16% (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).
Chronic post-prandial pain, weight loss or food fear before an acute-on-chronic thrombotic event (WSES 2022, Recommendation 2).
In ICU: unexplained abdominal distension, gastrointestinal bleeding, feed intolerance or rising vasopressor needs (WSES 2022, Recommendation 6).
physicalSigns: Soft abdomen early despite severe pain (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).
Peritonitis when bowel infarction has occurred (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).
Septic shock in late presentation (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).
Atrial fibrillation in about half of embolic cases (WSES 2022, Recommendation 2).
redFlags: Overt peritonitis: immediate laparoscopy or laparotomy (WSES 2022, Recommendation 9).
Abdominal pain with lactic acidosis in a patient who otherwise looks well: get CTA early (WSES 2022, Recommendation 4).
Critically ill patient on vasopressors with abdominal pain or distension and new organ failure: suspect NOMI (WSES 2022, Recommendation 6).
Every 6 hours of delay to CTA doubles mortality (WSES 2022, Recommendation 5).
precipitants: Atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, cardiac thrombus, mitral valve disease, endocarditis or previous embolism (WSES 2022, Table 1).
Diffuse atherosclerosis with post-prandial pain and weight loss (WSES 2022, Table 1).
Cardiac failure, low-flow states, vasopressors, dialysis and abdominal compartment syndrome for NOMI (WSES 2022, Table 1 and Recommendation 2).
Thrombophilia, oral contraceptives or oestrogen, portal hypertension, previous venous thromboembolism and pancreatitis for MVT (WSES 2022, Table 1).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Sudden severe pain and vomiting; atrial fibrillation or other cardiac source (WSES 2022, Table 1).
Progressive or sudden pain on a background of post-prandial pain and weight loss (WSES 2022, Table 1).
Critically ill, low-flow state, vasopressors; patent vessels on CTA (WSES 2022, Table 1 and Recommendation 5).
Progressive mild pain, thrombophilia or pancreatitis; superior mesenteric vein thrombus on venous-phase CTA (WSES 2022, Table 1 and Recommendation 5).
Amylase is raised in about half of AMI cases, so a raised amylase does not exclude AMI (WSES 2022, Recommendation 4).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Above 2 mmol/L; associated with irreversible ischaemia (hazard ratio 4.1)
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports suspicion but cannot separate early from irreversible ischaemia alone; lactic acidosis with abdominal pain should prompt early CTA (WSES 2022, Recommendation 4).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Mesenteric arteries and veins, bowel wall
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Arterial embolus or thrombus; superior mesenteric vein target sign in MVT; ischaemic bowel with patent vessels in NOMI
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Do without delay; no oral contrast; do not withhold for acute kidney injury (WSES 2022, Recommendation 5).
ruleIn.normalValue: Patent mesenteric vessels and normally enhancing bowel wall

clinicalManagement.title: Suspect and image
actions: Treat pain out of proportion to examination as AMI until proven otherwise (WSES 2022, Recommendation 1).
Send lactate, white cell count, D-dimer and electrolytes, and request CTA without delay (WSES 2022, Recommendations 4 and 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate
actions: Start fluid resuscitation with crystalloid and blood products, correct electrolytes and pass a nasogastric tube (WSES 2022, Recommendation 7).
Use vasopressors with caution; dobutamine, low-dose dopamine and milrinone have less effect on mesenteric flow (WSES 2022, Recommendation 7).
Use lactate trends to guide perfusion (WSES 2022, Recommendation 7).
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics at once (see Medicines) (WSES 2022, Recommendation 8).

clinicalManagement.title: Anticoagulate
actions: Start full-dose unfractionated heparin in all patients before the procedure (WSES 2022, Recommendation 9 discussion).
MVT without peritonitis: continuous heparin infusion is first-line and is often enough (WSES 2022, Recommendation 12).

clinicalManagement.title: Definitive treatment by type
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within hours; keep time to reperfusion short
actions: Peritonitis: laparoscopy or laparotomy to revascularise, resect non-viable bowel and keep viable bowel (WSES 2022, Recommendation 9).
Arterial occlusion: endovascular revascularisation first where expertise exists (WSES 2022, Recommendation 10).
Use damage control surgery with planned second look at 24 to 48 hours when viability is uncertain (WSES 2022, Recommendation 11).
NOMI: treat the cause, optimise cardiac output and stop vasopressors where possible; resect infarcted bowel (WSES 2022, Recommendation 13).
Haemodynamically normal patient without peritonitis in a hospital without the team: transfer to a specialised centre (WSES 2022, Figure 1).

clinicalManagement.title: Post-operative care
actions: Prefer noradrenaline with dobutamine over vasopressin for hypotension (WSES 2022, Recommendation 14).
Continue systemic heparin with aPTT 40 to 60 in all patients; therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin is an alternative if no further surgery is planned (WSES 2022, Recommendation 14).
Continue antibiotics at least 4 days in stable immunocompetent patients and tailor to cultures (WSES 2022, Recommendation 8).

clinicalManagement.title: Long-term plan
actions: After revascularisation: surveillance imaging by CTA or duplex within 6 months and long-term anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy (WSES 2022, Recommendation 18).
Massive necrosis in a frail patient: discuss goals of care including palliation (WSES 2022, Recommendation 17).

regimens.indication: Full-dose anticoagulation in AMI before and after surgery or intervention
regimens.dose: Full-dose regimen: 5000 units intravenously, then 20,000 to 40,000 units per 24 hours by continuous infusion in 1000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride, adjusted to the aPTT (Heparin label, Section 2.4).
regimens.duration: Until switched to long-term oral anticoagulation by the treating team (WSES 2022, Recommendation 18)
adjustments: Label target aPTT 1.5 to 2 times normal (Heparin label, Section 2.3); WSES post-operative aPTT 40 to 60 (WSES 2022, Recommendation 14).
Unfractionated heparin is easy to manage in acute kidney failure (WSES 2022, Recommendation 9 discussion).
Caution in liver disease with impaired haemostasis (Heparin label, Section 5.2).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: aPTT, international normalised ratio (INR) and platelets at baseline, then aPTT about every 4 hours (Heparin label, Section 2.3).
Potassium in renal failure (Heparin label, Section 5.9).
contraindications: History of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (Heparin label, Section 4).
Hypersensitivity to heparin or pork products (Heparin label, Section 4).
Uncontrolled active bleeding, except disseminated intravascular coagulation (Heparin label, Section 4).

regimens.indication: Broad-spectrum cover for bacterial translocation in AMI
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with AMI, severe intra-abdominal infection category
regimens.dose: 4.5 g intravenously every 6 hours (MOH IAI protocol, Table 2, severe infection or high risk); infuse over 30 minutes (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Section 2.1).
regimens.duration: At least 4 days in stable immunocompetent patients after source control; longer if infection persists (WSES 2022, Recommendation 8; MOH IAI protocol, Section Duration of Therapy)
adjustments: Creatinine clearance 40 mL/min or less, or dialysis: reduce the dose (label Table 1, other indications: 20 to 40 mL/min 2.25 g every 6 hours; under 20 mL/min 2.25 g every 8 hours; haemodialysis 2.25 g every 12 hours plus 0.75 g after each session) (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Section 2.3).
Sodium load 54 mg per gram of piperacillin; consider in heart failure (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Section 5).

branches.label: Confirmed or strongly suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia
branches.entryCriteria: Adult with CTA-confirmed or strongly suspected AMI of any type, no heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, no uncontrolled bleeding, no beta-lactam allergy.

medicationPlan.note: WSES 2022 names no doses. Heparin dose from the US label; antibiotic from the Saudi MOH intra-abdominal infection (IAI) protocol severe column, which also lists meropenem 1 g every 8 hours and imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg every 6 hours (MOH IAI protocol, Table 2). The MOH and label piperacillin–tazobactam doses differ; see comparison. diagnosticCriteria.threshold: CTA without delay in any patient with suspected AMI, interpreted with the clinical picture; no laboratory test confirms or excludes it (WSES 2022, Recommendations 4 and 5).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Signs of irreversible ischaemia on CTA
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Bowel dilatation and wall thickening, reduced or absent wall enhancement, pneumatosis, portal venous gas and free air (WSES 2022, Recommendation 5).

teaching.scope: Adults with suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI) in the emergency department (ED), surgical ward or intensive care unit (ICU): recognition of the four types (arterial embolism, arterial thrombosis, non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia and mesenteric venous thrombosis), laboratory tests, computed tomography angiography (CTA), resuscitation, heparin, antibiotics and the surgical or endovascular pathway. Uses the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) 2022 guideline, the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) intra-abdominal infection protocol and US product labels. Operative technique is for the surgical team and is summarised only.
learningObjectives: Suspect AMI when pain is out of proportion to signs.
Get CTA without delay, even with acute kidney injury.
Resuscitate, anticoagulate and give antibiotics before definitive treatment.
Match treatment to type: embolus, thrombosis, NOMI or venous thrombosis.
pitfalls: Diagnosing pancreatitis from a raised amylase.
Withholding CTA contrast because of kidney injury.
Using high-dose vasopressors that worsen NOMI.
keyPoints: No blood test excludes AMI; a normal D-dimer makes it unlikely.
Endovascular revascularisation first for arterial occlusion where available.

patientEducation: Your bowel lost its blood supply; surgery or a procedure may be needed to restore flow.
After discharge, take blood thinners as prescribed and attend scans.
Seek help at once for new severe abdominal pain.
lifestyleAndDiet: Stop smoking and treat high cholesterol, blood pressure and diabetes (WSES 2022, Recommendation 18).
mdtReferrals: Emergency or general surgeon; vascular surgeon; interventional radiologist; intensivist (WSES 2022, Recommendation 15); dietitian and intestinal failure team for short bowel (WSES 2022, Recommendation 16).
dischargeCriteria: Bowel viable after second look; tolerating diet or nutrition plan in place; anticoagulation or antiplatelet plan agreed; surveillance imaging booked within 6 months after revascularisation (WSES 2022, Recommendation 18).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: CTA or duplex surveillance within 6 months after revascularisation, then regular follow-up; long-term anticoagulation, with lifelong treatment considered for thrombophilia (WSES 2022, Recommendation 18).
